name: Hotelworld AI: AI Search Visibility Research and Agents for Hotels
title: Hotelworld AI: AI Search Visibility Research and Agents for Hotels
answer: Hotelworld AI is a hospitality technology company, founded in 2024, that publishes the World's Best at AI Index and sells modular AI agents for hotels. Its most useful finding for anyone following AI in hospitality is that only about one in six of the world's hotel properties, 130,884 of roughly 810,000, currently appear in AI-generated search responses, making answer-engine visibility a measurable competitive metric.

sections.body: Hotelworld AI Limited is a company founded in 2024 that builds AI agents for hotels and publishes research on how hotels appear in AI-generated recommendations. Its website combines product pages for its agents, guidance blog posts on AI-driven search, case studies, partnership news, and download pages for its World's Best at AI Index reports. The Q1 2026 index update and the 2025 index are the main research documents described. The site also carries a privacy policy covering GDPR, CCPA and EU AI Act compliance.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The research reports measure how often hotels appear in AI-generated answers across ChatGPT, Google AI and Perplexity. The 2025 index states that only one sixth of the world's hotel properties, 130,884 of about 810,000, are visible in AI-generated search responses, with Holiday Inn Express leading globally ahead of Ibis Hotels and Hilton. The Q1 2026 update tracks 2,105 or more hotel brands and 131,000 properties, reports Hilton within four points of becoming the most visible brand, Hyatt nearly doubling its index score as the fastest-growing major brand, and the threshold to stay in the global top 25 rising 25 percent in one quarter. It puts consistency of AI recommendations for top properties at about 90 percent. The guidance posts argue that AI systems assemble answers from trusted, well-structured sources, and set out practices such as Schema.org structured data, answer-first page architecture, content clusters and consistent name, address and phone data. The company's Leo agent tracks AI visibility, applies geo-stamping across more than 30 countries and tests multi-turn interpretation, while Iris predicts demand from more than 50 sources.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states that only 1 in 6 hotels are visible to AI search, that 130,884 of roughly 810,000 properties appear in AI-generated responses, that the Q1 2026 index covers 2,105 or more brands and 131,000 properties, that the top-25 threshold rose 25 percent in a quarter, that AI recommendations are about 90 percent consistent for top properties, that almost half of brands are misaligned between desired category and AI perception, that The Ritz-Carlton scores 37.58 globally but 96.63 in MEA, that AI surfaces only 3 to 5 answers per query against 10 to 20 links on Google, that one Mayfair hotel saw a 38 percent visibility increase over six months, and that an estimated 60 to 70 percent of searches end without a click.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For a reader following AI in hospitality, this source turns AI-assistant visibility into a tracked competitive metric with named leaders, movers and thresholds. It supplies the numbers behind the claim that only a small minority of hotels appear in AI-generated shortlists, and it describes the practices, structured data, answer-first content and consistent business data, that the company says influence whether a hotel is surfaced. The case study and agent descriptions show how visibility is monitored in practice, including geo-stamping across markets and testing how assistants interpret a brand in multi-turn conversations.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Hospitality

sections.body: The research is published by a company selling the agents it describes, so the index findings and the guidance serve its commercial interest. Several report pages are download forms rather than full documents, so much of the underlying methodology is not visible on the site. The index covers brand-level visibility rather than booking or revenue outcomes, and the case study reports a single unnamed hotel. The site gives no independent verification of its figures.
